title: Pentagon Locks In Seven-Year SM-3 Supply Deals With Boeing and RTX as Interceptor Replenishment Drags On
subhead: The Pentagon signed seven-year framework agreements with Boeing and RTX to expand production of Standard Missile-3 components, part of a broader push to put the defense industrial base on a wartime footing after the Iran war drained interceptor stockpiles. Separately, Lockheed and Raytheon are stalling on the promised Patriot license for Ukraine, and CENTCOM stood up a multinational attack-drone task force.

sections.heading: Pentagon Locks In SM-3 Supply With Boeing and RTX
sections.body:
The Pentagon signed two seven-year framework agreements with Boeing and RTX on Friday to expand production of critical components for the Standard Missile-3, the Navy's primary ship-launched ballistic missile interceptor, Defense News reports. The deals cover avionics and ejector assemblies Boeing supplies to prime contractor Raytheon for both the SM-3 Block IB and the newer Block IIA, which operate with the Aegis Ballistic Missile Defense System to destroy incoming missiles outside the atmosphere.

The frameworks let Boeing begin building components before a contract is in place while the three sides negotiate a multiyear deal, giving suppliers the demand certainty to invest in added capacity. Neither the Pentagon nor Boeing released dollar figures or quantities. Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment Michael P. Duffey said the agreements are about 'stabilizing our supply chains, expanding munitions production and putting our entire defense industrial base on a wartime footing.'

The move mirrors a seven-year deal Boeing struck in April to triple production of PAC-3 seeker components, and follows the Missile Defense Agency's award earlier this month of a $745 million contract to Raytheon for fully assembled SM-3 Block IIA interceptors for the United States and Japan. The Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated the SM-3 inventory at 414 as of December 2025, with wartime expenditures of between 130 and 250 missiles and replenishment expected to take years.
sections.whyItMatters: The Pentagon is shifting from buying finished interceptors to locking in subcontractor capacity years ahead, a recognition that the Iran war exposed how thin the missile supply chain really is. The SM-3 line is now a strategic bottleneck, not just a procurement line.

sections.heading: Patriot License for Ukraine Stalls as US Giants Hedge
sections.body:
Though President Donald Trump promised Kyiv a license to build Patriot interceptors at the July NATO summit in Ankara, Lockheed Martin and Raytheon have put the brakes on a joint-production deal, Defense News reports. Executives are weighing what is 'feasible' and the licensing is running into Washington red tape, even as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy posted on X that the two sides have 'now reached an agreement.'

A Republican official on Capitol Hill told The Atlantic that the real worry is not technology theft but competition: 'Their real worry is that the Ukrainians will find a way to improve the Patriot and then produce them at scale faster and for much less money than what the existing production lines in the U.S. could do.' The companies will publicly frame concerns around IP theft and tech transfer instead, the official said.

The context is a booming Ukrainian defense industry and a parallel European effort. Five days after Trump's pledge, Ukraine, nine European countries and defense heavyweights including Eurosam, Leonardo, Thales and Saab launched a coalition in Paris to field Freyja, an entirely new antiballistic system built around a Ukrainian interceptor priced at roughly one-fifth of a Patriot round. A week later Lockheed unveiled its own cheaper PAC-3 ACE at Farnborough, advertised at roughly $2 million a round — less than half the price of the round Ukraine currently fires.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between Trump's political promise and what the two US primes will actually do reveals the core tension of the moment: Washington wants Ukraine armed, but the incumbents who dominate antiballistic missile production have little incentive to create a cheaper competitor that could undercut their monopoly.

sections.heading: CENTCOM Stands Up Multinational Attack-Drone Task Force
sections.body:
U.S. Central Command announced it will stand up Task Force Falcon Strike, its first task force focused on multi-domain, multinational attack drones, Defense News reports. The unit will employ one-way attack drones composed of unmanned systems from above, on and below the sea, managed by U.S. military support staff and regional partners. Personnel from U.S. Special Operations Command Central will lead the staff.

The move follows CENTCOM's establishment of Task Force Scorpion Strike in December 2025, a Middle East-based unit that was the first to launch an aerial attack drone from a U.S. Navy warship and deployed one-way systems during Operation Epic Fury and strikes on Iranian port facilities in July. Adm. Brad Cooper, CENTCOM commander, said Falcon Strike will 'expand on Scorpion Strike's success given the tremendous innovation happening among our regional allies and partners.' The release did not specify which regional partners are involved.

The announcement comes as the U.S. continues its war with Iran, which has depleted U.S. munitions stockpiles and pushed military leaders to weigh cheaper anti-drone and one-way attack systems at a faster pace.
sections.whyItMatters: CENTCOM is institutionalizing the one-way attack drone as a core warfighting tool and, crucially, folding regional partners into it. This is a shift from buying drones to building a multinational drone-operating architecture in the Middle East.

sections.heading: DARPA Wants a Hypersonic Cruise Missile That Can Dodge Air Defenses
sections.body:
DARPA has issued a Request for Information for a Next Generation Hypersonic Cruise Missile (NGHCM), a scramjet-powered weapon designed to evade enemy interceptors, Defense News reports. The RFI, due October 6, warns that the rapid proliferation of advanced Integrated Air Defense Systems 'threaten to restrict the operational freedom of U.S. forces and diminish the effectiveness of current stand-off strike capabilities.'

DARPA wants a demonstrator that is both survivable and affordable enough to be manufactured in large quantities, with a focus on range, cruise speed and altitude. The RFI lists potential launch platforms from tactical fighters and heavy bombers to surface-based vertical launch systems and 'Heavy Ground-Launch / Strategic Defense Class' platforms. It asks companies to identify an accelerated schedule to reach first flight rather than relying on traditional acquisition models, and to address testing across missions from 250 to 2,000 nautical miles. DARPA said it 'strongly encourages responses from non-traditional defense contractors and emerging technology developers.'
sections.whyItMatters: The program is a direct response to the Iran war, where U.S. air defenses intercepted Iranian missiles but the Pentagon grew concerned its own missiles are vulnerable to peer air defenses. The emphasis on affordability and non-traditional contractors signals a push to make hypersonics a mass-producible weapon, not a boutique one.

sections.heading: Russian Air Bridge to the Sahel Keeps Flowing, C4ADS Finds
sections.body:
Russian state-aligned military forces operating in the Central Sahel relied on at least 75 flights by military and military-linked aircraft between January 2025 and July 2026, according to a new analysis by the Center for Advanced Defense Studies, Defense News reports. The report examined ADS-B data from FlightRadar24 for aircraft models historically linked to Russian private military contractors or the Ministry of Defense, filtering for flights touching Mali, Burkina Faso or Niger.

Burkina Faso received the most flights at 56, followed by 38 to Mali and six to Niger. The busiest single operator was Flight Unit 224, a Russian Ministry of Defense-owned airline sanctioned by the U.S. in May 2023. The Russian Special Flight Squadron conducted 14 flights and the Ministry for Emergency Situations 12, despite the ministry's ostensibly humanitarian mandate. C4ADS flagged several private carriers it said remain unsanctioned despite documented links to Russian military logistics, including Kyrgyzstan-registered Sapsan Airlines. State-owned aircraft typically refueled at Russia's Khmeimim air base in Syria and Libyan sites before continuing to the Sahel.
sections.whyItMatters: The air bridge shows Russia's Africa Corps footprint in the Sahel is sustained by a logistics network that runs through sanctioned state airlines and still-unsanctioned private carriers. The report's finding that flights increasingly transit Togo and Algeria points to a widening network that sanctions have not closed.

sections.heading: Australia Becomes First Export Customer for AIM-260; Japan White Paper Warns of 'New Era of Crisis'
sections.body:
Australia will become the first export customer for the AIM-260A Joint Advanced Tactical Missile (JATM), the classified Lockheed Martin air-to-air missile, Defense News reports. Defence Minister Richard Marles announced the purchase on Aug. 6 at the Pitch Black 2026 exercise in Darwin. Canberra will spend A$736 million (about $520 million USD) on an unspecified quantity through Foreign Military Sales, well under the 450 JATMs and $3.16 billion the U.S. approved in March — suggesting a first tranche of under 100 missiles. The AIM-260 will be integrated first onto the RAAF's F/A-18F Super Hornet, then the F-35A and EA-18G Growler, with the MQ-28A Ghost Bat a likely future candidate. Its range is likely at least 120 miles, far beyond the incumbent AIM-120 AMRAAM, which is now outclassed by China's PL-15 and PL-17.

Separately, Japan's 2026 Defense White Paper declared the international community is 'entering a new era of crisis' and called China the 'greatest strategic challenge,' citing Beijing's growing concordance with Moscow, Defense News reports. The paper emphasized lower-cost systems, increased production and stockpiling, and Japan's acquisition of large numbers of low-cost unmanned vehicles across air, sea and underwater domains to establish its SHIELD littoral defense concept by FY 2027. It also flagged that some Japanese companies like Komatsu and Mitsui have abandoned or downsized their defense involvement.
sections.whyItMatters: Australia's JATM purchase is a significant trust signal — Washington is exporting its most classified air-to-air weapon to a first foreign customer as a hedge against China's long-range missiles. Japan's white paper, meanwhile, shows Tokyo doubling down on low-cost unmanned systems and domestic industrial capacity as it moves toward taking primary responsibility for its own defense.

bottomLine: Today's developments center on the industrial consequences of the Iran war. The Pentagon is locking in multi-year subcontractor capacity for SM-3 interceptors rather than just buying finished missiles, while the promised Patriot license for Ukraine stalls as Lockheed and Raytheon weigh the competitive threat of a cheaper Ukrainian-built interceptor. CENTCOM is institutionalizing multinational attack-drone operations, DARPA wants a mass-producible hypersonic cruise missile, and the Russian air bridge to the Sahel keeps running through sanctioned and unsanctioned carriers alike. In Asia, Australia becomes the first export customer for the classified AIM-260 and Japan's white paper signals a deeper pivot to low-cost unmanned systems and domestic production. The through-line: the war has turned missile and drone supply chains into the central strategic battleground.
